newsitem.title: BOSNIA: West lacks leverage over hardline Bosnian Serbs.
newsitem.headline: West lacks leverage over hardline Bosnian Serbs.

text.p: A Serb boycott of the first session of Bosnia's peacetime parliament demonstrated how Western powers lack effective leverage over hardline nationalists, analysts and diplomats said on Monday.

Foreign dignitaries, including a senior envoy sent by U.S. President Bill Clinton, waited for more than three hours on Saturday for Serb representatives to appear at the inauguration ceremony in Sarajevo's national theatre.
The Serbs never showed up, refusing to publicly display support for Bosnian statehood but claiming security reasons.
For the Serbs, signing an oath of loyalty to uphold the Bosnian constitution would have amounted to a renunciation of their war aims to carve out a separate state.
The boycott, which humiliated Western envoys, underscored the Serbs' determination to stick to their separatist ideology and dictate terms for the post-war government.
Diplomats admitted privately that the United States and European governments have no big stick at their disposal to force the Bosnian Serbs to come to heel.
Economic sanctions were formally lifted last week against Serbia and Bosnia's Serb republic to reward Belgrade for its endorsement of the Dayton peace agreement.
The West maintains an "outer wall" of sanctions against Serbia, sponsors of the Bosnian Serbs, blocking access to vital capital from international financial institutions.
Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic would like the "outer wall" of sanctions removed but his Bosnian Serb proteges seem more interested in obstructing attempts to reunify Bosnia.
Western powers have sought out the Serbian leader in the past to press him to force compliance from the Bosnian Serbs.
But Milosevic now portrays himself as an outsider when it comes to the Bosnian Serbs, after elections in Bosnia in which his Socialist proxies were defeated, diplomats said.

"Milosevic maintains he has fulfilled his commitments under the peace agreement and says he can't control what happens in Pale," the base for the Bosnian Serb leadership, said one diplomat who asked not to be named.
"He's keeping his distance."
The office for the international High Representative to Bosnia, which organised the ceremony, said the Bosnian Serbs would not be wooed to rejoin the peace process.
"Now the ball is in their court and we will wait to see if that ball is played back to us," said Colum Murphy, a spokesman for the High Representative, Carl Bildt.
Murphy said the Bosnian Serbs could not push for a separate state with impunity.
"If it is true that they seek secession we do have very important leverage in that diplomatic and political recognition would be withheld."
Now that they have made their point, Serb leaders will probably attend the next parliamentary session, whenever it is scheduled, analysts said.
But the Serbs may take their time about agreeing the details of the next session to make clear they posess the power to block the body when it suits them.
Analysts predicted Western envoys would soon be forced to drive up to the mountain village of Pale, the Bosnian Serb government seat, to bargain.

"What we are going to see is highly embarrassing diplomacy, big countries sending senior people to meet trumped-up thugs essentially to get them to meet up with each other," said Chris Bennett, a spokesman for the International Crisis Group, a private agency monitoring the peace process.
Bennett said major powers were pouring tremendous resources into Bosnia without imposing harsh penalties on rival factions if they flouted international obligations.
"Having given up sanctions, we've given up the biggest stick we had," he said. "We need to get seriously tough with all sides."
